title: Colour-coded cloths: a business-set system that keeps areas apart
audience: Cleaners who set up and use cloths and tools across more than one area of a site.
learningOutcomes: Explain why separate cloths for separate areas prevent cross-contamination.
Read the business's colour key and apply it without assuming a colour's meaning from another business.
Remove from use and replace a cloth that has crossed into an area it was not assigned to.

instruction.heading: What the colour system is for
instruction.body: A colour system keeps cloths, mops and tools tied to one area of a site, so that soil, micro-organisms or product residue collected in one area does not travel to another. The colour itself does not protect anyone. The protection comes from the rule that each colour is used only in its assigned area and is not swapped between areas during a job. A cloth used in a washroom is safe to keep in use only while it stays in the washroom.

instruction.heading: Each business sets its own colours
instruction.body: Colour meanings differ between businesses, between sites and sometimes between clients. One example scheme assigns one colour to toilets and urinals, another to general areas, and a third to food-preparation areas. A different business may use a different set of colours for the same areas, or may use shapes, labels or bag colours instead. Do not assume a colour's meaning from anything you have seen elsewhere. The colour key is set by management, recorded in the business's procedures and shown at the site or on the job sheet. If the key is missing for a site, ask before you start.

instruction.heading: Setting up cloths and tools by area
instruction.body: Before you start, list the areas you will clean and check that each has its own set of cloths and tools. Keep the sets apart in the kit or on the trolley so that you cannot reach into the wrong set without noticing. Label holders or bags where the business uses them. Do not carry a loose cloth in a pocket or on your shoulder between areas. A cloth that drops on the floor is no longer clean for any area, so set it aside and take a replacement from the correct set.

instruction.heading: Working between areas
instruction.body: Work through the area order the business sets, which is usually from the cleanest area toward the dirtiest. When you move from one area to the next, do not carry a used tool across the threshold. Change gloves or wash your hands as your procedure requires before you handle cloths for a different area. Before each move, ask one question: is this cloth, mop or tool assigned to the area I am about to enter? If the answer is not clear, do not use it there.

instruction.heading: Recognising a crossed cloth and recovering
instruction.body: A cloth has crossed when it has been used in an area it is not assigned to, has touched a surface from another area, or has dropped onto a floor that you have not yet cleaned. Take it out of use and keep it apart from your clean cloths until it is handled the way the business directs. Clean the affected surface again with a correctly assigned cloth, then record the event and tell your supervisor, following the business's correction procedure. Do not decide on your own that the transfer was harmless.

procedure: Confirm the colour key or the cloth-to-area mapping with the supervisor or the job record before setting up.
Set out a separate, labelled cloth and tool set for each area you will clean.
Keep the sets apart in the kit so you cannot reach into the wrong set.
Work the area order the business sets, and ask before each move whether the item is assigned to the next area.
Take any cloth that has crossed areas out of use and keep it apart from clean cloths.
Re-clean the affected surface with an assigned cloth and record the event.

workedExamples.situation: You are cleaning a bathroom in a short-stay property. You wipe the basin with the cloth you have just used on the toilet exterior, then wipe the kitchen bench in the same room with that cloth.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What has happened, and what do you do next?
workedExamples.reasoning: The cloth has moved from a sanitary area to a general area and has touched a surface outside its assigned zone. Stop, set the cloth aside, and re-clean the basin and the bench with clean cloths from the correct sets. Record the event and tell the supervisor. Check which cloth set the business assigns to the basin before you continue.

workedExamples.situation: A colleague offers you a cloth from their own kit because yours have run out. They say the colour does not matter because the surface is only a cupboard door.
workedExamples.reasoning: Decline the cloth. The colour key is a rule for keeping areas apart, not a judgement about how dirty a surface looks. Ask the supervisor for the correct set or for a clean cloth assigned to that area, and report the shortage so the kit can be restocked.

workedExamples.situation: You arrive at a new site where the job sheet has no colour key, and the business's procedure says to ask before starting.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do before setting up?
workedExamples.reasoning: Ask the supervisor to confirm the colour key or the assigned cloth sets. Do not guess from another business's colours. Once it is confirmed, record the key on the job sheet so that the next worker does not need to ask.

equipmentAndPpe: One labelled cloth and tool set for each assigned area, as the business sets
Separate holders, bags or trays for each set
Gloves changed, or hands washed, between areas as the procedure requires
Written colour key or cloth-to-area mapping on the job sheet

commonErrors.error: Assuming a colour means the same thing in every business.
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm the colour key from the job sheet or the supervisor before setting up.

commonErrors.error: Using the nearest cloth because the right set is out of reach.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep the sets in separate holders and ask for a replacement rather than cross-using.

commonErrors.error: Treating a colour as if it were a sanitising step.
commonErrors.prevention: The colour keeps areas apart. Cleaning and any sanitising are separate steps set by the business procedure.

commonErrors.error: Continuing to use a cloth after it has been dropped on a floor.
commonErrors.prevention: Set it aside, replace it from the correct set, and re-clean the affected surface.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Colour meanings are set by each business. This lesson teaches the principle of keeping areas apart, not a universal colour scheme. No colour is a regulatory standard.
Where a site is a food premises, follow the site's food safety program.
Product use follows the label and the safety data sheet, not the colour of the cloth.

qualityStandard: Each area is served by its assigned cloth set, with no cross-use during the job.
The colour key is confirmed before setup and recorded on the job sheet.
Any crossed cloth is taken out of use, the affected surface is re-cleaned, and the event is recorded.
documentationEvidence: Colour key or cloth-to-area mapping on the job sheet.
Record of any cross-area event, the correction made and who was told.
summary: A colour keeps areas apart. It does not sanitise anything.
Each business sets its own colour key, and you confirm it before you start.
Keep the sets apart, move only assigned items, and never cross-use.
If a cloth crosses areas, take it out of use, re-clean with an assigned cloth, and record the event.

knowledgeChecks.question: When a business uses coloured cloths, what keeps a surface from being contaminated by another area?
options: The colour itself kills germs on the surface once the cloth has been used on it
The rule that each colour stays in its assigned area and is not swapped during the job
Using the same cloth for every area, since the colour is only a guide

knowledgeChecks.question: You arrive at a site with no colour key. What is the correct action?
options: Assume red is for washrooms because it is the most common choice
Use the colour scheme from the last business you worked for
Ask the supervisor to confirm the key or the assigned sets before setting up

knowledgeChecks.question: A cloth used on a toilet exterior has been dropped on the floor of a general area. What do you do?
options: Set it aside, re-clean the affected surface with an assigned cloth, and record the event
Rinse it and keep using it in the general area for the rest of the shift without washing it
Use it only on the floor because it is already dirty and nobody will check it
